det.desc: A silver-plated Old Master pattern candy dish by Towle. The estimate for this Towle silver-plated candy dish to be valued between $10-$20 USD. Silversmiths in Newburyport, Massachusetts, often crafted decorative serving pieces like this to bring traditional elegance into everyday middle-class homes. They were made during the mid-20th century to serve sweets, nuts, or small candies during formal gatherings and family celebrations. Craftsmen created these pieces by stamping base metal alloys with heavy hydraulic presses before applying a fine layer of silver plate and detailed hand-buffing. Middle-class families used them on coffee tables, sideboards, and dining tables during holidays and special visits. Over time, as formal entertaining declined and modern stainless steel became popular for daily use, these decorative silver-plated dishes transitioned from dining tables to enclosed display cabinets.

rows.t: Antique Lozi Bowl,  Nesting Duck- Authentic Hand Carved African Hardwood

det.desc: This striking, authentic Lozi lidded food bowl is a premier example of mid-to-late 20th-century African utilitarian art. Hand-carved from a single, solid block of dense, rich African hardwood by the Lozi people of the Western Province (historically Barotseland) along the Zambezi River valley in Zambia, this mid-to-large-sized vessel features a beautifully streamlined silhouette topped with a stylized swimming duck finial that serves as a functional handle. Historically used to serve prepared meats and vegetables while keeping them warm, these bowls are highly prized today by collectors of global folk art, ethnographic artifacts, and organic mid-century modern design. The piece displays incredible, traditional craftsmanship. The thin, stepped inner lip of the lid is meticulously carved to form a flush, interlocking seal with the base. Inside, the continuous, rhythmic adze gouge marks remain clearly visible across the interior walls, proving it was hollowed entirely by hand rather than turned on a mechanical lathe.
